title: How to close a sales call: 7 Steps for small businesses
summary: Wondering how to close a sales call without sounding pushy? Use these 7 steps, real scripts, and follow-up tips to book more jobs from the calls you get.
body_markdown:
Here’s a familiar situation: a homeowner calls about a leaking water heater. You ask about what’s going on, suggest a fix, and give her a price. Then you wrap up with a familiar question: “Anything else for today?”


“No, that’s it. Let me talk to my husband and call you back.”


You hope she’ll call back. By Thursday, you’re still waiting. Meanwhile, she found another plumber on Google and booked with them.


Closing a sales call isn’t about making a big ask at the end of the call. It starts when you pick up the phone, and it’s built in small commitments across the whole call.


At Quo, we analyzed over 2,000 of our own sales calls to find out which closing strategies work better than others. We found that the same patterns keep showing up.


In this article, we’ll share those patterns so you can close your sales calls successfully. We’ll walk you through seven steps to get there so that you can take customers from the first call to a booked job.


Here are the seven steps of closing a sales call. Click on any of the steps to jump to that section of the article.


1. [Be ready before the phone rings](https://www.quo.com/blog/how-to-close-a-sales-call/#be-ready)
2. [Qualify the job](https://www.quo.com/blog/how-to-close-a-sales-call/#qualify)
3. [Explain the fix or service, then check in](https://www.quo.com/blog/how-to-close-a-sales-call/#explain)
4. [Give a price or range, and ask if it works](https://www.quo.com/blog/how-to-close-a-sales-call/#pricing)
5. [Surface concerns before you ask for the booking](https://www.quo.com/blog/how-to-close-a-sales-call/#surface-concerns)
6. [Ask for the booking](https://www.quo.com/blog/how-to-close-a-sales-call/#booking)
7. [Book it, confirm it, remind them](https://www.quo.com/blog/how-to-close-a-sales-call/#confirm-and-remind)


##


What does it mean to close a sales call?


Closing a sales call means getting the customer to commit to a specific next step that moves your jobs forward.


What that commitment looks like depends on the type of call:


- **New lead asking for a quote.** Booking an estimate, site visit, or job.
- **Estimate or consultation.** Getting the estimate approved, collecting a deposit, or getting a signed agreement.
- **Follow-up on an estimate.** Getting a clear yes or no. If they agree, booking a date.
- **Existing customer.** Booking another service, maintenance plan, or recurring work.


Your sales closing strategy comes down to knowing what commitment you’re asking for and when to ask for it. Closing a sales call isn’t always the same as closing the deal. Booking an estimate or site visit still counts, even if the customer hasn’t agreed to the full job yet.


### Early in the call: Qualify the job


On our own sales calls, questions about the customer’s timeline and who makes the decision came up about 40% of the way through, before pricing.


*“Do you have a timeline in mind?”* is the closing question our team asks the most. It doesn’t ask the customer to commit to anything, but it does help lay the groundwork for closing the sale.


For a service business, you might ask:


- *When do you need this done? This can help you gauge how urgent their need is.*
- *Is this your home, or are you renting? This confirms whether they can decide on a renovation project or whether they may need approval for it.*


For more on this stage of the sales process, see our guides to the[discovery call](https://www.quo.com/blog/discovery-call/) and[BANT sales](https://www.quo.com/blog/bant-sales/) .


### After you explain the fix or service: Check that it lands


As soon as you’ve explained what you’d do, stop and check in. On a call, you can’t see them nodding along, so you have to ask. For example:


- Does that sound like what you’re dealing with?
- Would that work for your schedule?


If they say yes, then they’re comfortable with how you plan to handle the job. If they hesitate or seem unsure, ask what’s concerning them and address their questions before moving forward.


### The final minutes: Book it


Once you’ve given them a price, find out if anything is holding them back before asking for the booking:


- Anything you’d want to go over before we book?
- Would you like me to book a time for you?


If they have a concern, you want to hear it while you can answer it. Once you’ve talked it through, you can get a date on the calendar.


### Why the last minute is the weakest place to close


Rewind to our example scenario: “Anything else for today?” led the lead to check in with her husband and not call back.


If you try to end your call with a closing question, you’re likely to fall short.


By then, the call is wrapping up, leaving little time to address a concern or set a date. So the close needs to happen earlier. Save the last minute for confirming what you’ve agreed on: the date, the time, and what happens next.


### Buying signals that mean it’s time to ask


Pay attention to what a caller asks you. They might want to know when you can take on their job, whether you offer financing, or whether you’ve done a job like theirs before. Those are signs they’re thinking about hiring you.


You’ll also hear a sense of urgency in what some callers tell you: no heat, a leak, a court date next month, or a move-out inspection coming up.


Compare that with someone who opens with “What do you charge?” without telling you anything about the job. They’re likely calling around for quotes. Gracie Ouyang, an account executive at Quo, has a rule of thumb: **Callers who describe what’s broken are buying. Those who lead with price are comparing.**


That won’t be true for every caller, but our team sees it a lot. When you hear buying signals like estimated timeline and job experience , that’s your cue to ask for the job.


##


How to close a sales call in 7 steps


So how do you turn an interested caller into a booked appointment or job? These seven steps walk you through the process, from getting ready before the phone rings to confirming the booking.


### 1. Be ready before the phone rings


Callers often have two questions: How much will the job cost, and when can you send someone out?


Keep those in mind during your[sales call planning](https://www.quo.com/blog/sales-call-planning/) . Have your price ranges and available appointment times handy, so you’re not saying, *“Let me call you back.”*


If you need to see a job in person before quoting it, explain what the visit involves and whether there’s a fee. And if someone wants an appointment tomorrow, check your calendar before you say yes.


For returning customers, pull up the details of their previous job when they call. A quick *“Is this the furnace we serviced in January?”* saves them from having to explain their service history again.


But even with everything ready, you won’t catch every call when you’re busy on a job. Pick up quickly when you can, since customers may call businesses they find on Google until someone answers. As Gracie puts it, “We know typically a missed call does cost you money.” Home service businesses miss around 27% of their inbound calls, according to[Invoca data cited by Housecall Pro](https://www.housecallpro.com/resources/missed-calls/) .


For calls you can’t take, set up a backup routing option. An automatic text after a missed call lets customers know you got their call. Quo’s[Sona](https://www.quo.com/sona) AI agent can also answer when you’re on a job or after hours and collect the details you need.


##


Pro tip: Use this pre-call checklist


- Prices or ranges for your most common jobs


- Your next three available openings


- Your service area and any trip or diagnostic fees


- The caller’s history, if they’ve worked with you before


- An estimate template or booking link ready to text


- Backup coverage for calls you can’t answer, like a teammate or an AI agent


### 2. Qualify the job


[Lead qualification](https://www.quo.com/blog/lead-qualification/) starts with understanding what the caller needs. Ask, *“What’s going on, and how long has it been happening?”* Then find out what they’ve already tried.


Use their answers to figure out three things:


- **How urgent is it?** Water spreading across the basement floor needs help right away. A routine faucet replacement can usually wait until next week.
- **Can you take the job?** Make sure you offer the service and cover the customer’s area. If you don’t, tell them now instead of booking a visit you’ll have to cancel.
- **Who else needs to approve it?** Ask, “Do you need to run this by anyone else first?” If a homeowner needs to discuss a big repair with their spouse, offer to go over the options with both of them.


If you run a law firm, your checks look a little different. Confirm the type of case it is and who else is involved, then screen for conflicts of interest before proceeding with a consultation.


When you’re setting up Sona to answer your calls, you can choose the questions it asks new leads. Their answers appear in a call summary, so your team has what they need for the follow-up conversation.


### 3. Explain the fix or service, then check in


Tell the caller what you’d do next in plain language, without industry jargon or a long explanation. You can’t promise a fix before you’ve seen the problem, so explain what the visit will cover.


For a leaking water heater, it might sound like: *“We’ll come out, check the tank and the connections, and find where the leak is coming from. Then we’ll go over whether it needs a repair or a replacement before we touch anything. Does that sound like a good plan?”*


Over the phone, you can’t see how the caller reacts to your explanation. The check-in lets them correct anything you got wrong before you discuss prices.


### 4. Give a price or range, and ask if it works


With the plan settled, it’s time to talk about your fees. If you know the usual range for this kind of job, share it. You could say, *“Most jobs like this run between $X and $Y, depending on what we find. Does that work for your budget?”*


If you can’t price it without seeing it, tell them what the visit costs and what it covers. If you charge more for after-hours or emergency visits, mention that too.


If your business credits the visit fee toward the repair, say so, along with any conditions, like booking the repair the same day. And let them know you won’t start any work until they’ve approved a price.


When they’re comfortable with the number, you can move the conversation from whether the job fits their budget to when it can happen.


### 5. Surface concerns before you ask for the booking


Even if the caller sounds interested, they might still have doubts about moving forward. You can find out what’s on their mind with a couple of[sales closing questions](https://www.quo.com/blog/sales-closing-questions/) :


- *“Anything holding you back from getting this on the schedule?”*
- *“Any concerns about the price or timing?”*


Give them a second to answer without filling the pause with another sales pitch. If the price is putting them off, explain what they’re paying for rather than rushing to offer a discount. If the available times don’t work, check for another opening.


It can feel easier to skip these questions and go straight to booking, but that won’t make their concerns disappear. You might end up waiting for a callback that never comes.


### 6. Ask for the booking


Before you book the lead for an estimate visit or your service, run through this checklist:


- **Timeline.** Do you know when they need the job done?
- **Decision-maker.** Do you know who needs to approve it?
- **Price.** Have they heard a price or range?
- **Concerns.** Have you asked about anything holding them back?


If they answered no to any of these questions, go back and discuss that topic. If all four are yes, ask directly: *“Would you like me to get you on the schedule?”* For a law firm, that might mean asking, *“Should I send over the engagement agreement?”*


### 7. Book it, confirm it, remind them


When the caller says yes to a booking, agree on a date and an arrival window. If it’s an in-person appointment, double-check the address and ask about any special access instructions.. For bigger jobs, you might also require a deposit. Walk them through the amount, the due date, and your cancellation terms before you collect it.


Some callers may want to run it by someone else, like a partner or landlord. Gracie’s fix is to put a time on the calendar anyway: *“Let’s pencil in Thursday. I can move it if you need to.”* Make it clear the time is tentative, and agree on when they’ll let you know.


At this stage, we recommend using an open-ended question like *“What would be the ideal next steps for you?”* It can help you understand what the customer has in mind and who else may be involved.


Before you hang up, text a confirmation with your business name, the service, the date and arrival window, the address, and a way to request changes. For example:


*“Hi Sarah, it’s Main Street Plumbing. You’re booked for a water heater repair on Thursday, 9 to 11 a.m., at 42 Oak Lane. Reply to this text to make any changes.”*


The day before the visit, send a reminder so customers don’t double-book before your team arrives. Schedule this follow-up when you make the booking, and it becomes part of your[customer follow-up system](https://www.quo.com/blog/customer-follow-up-system/) .


##


How to handle objections at the close


An objection near the end of a call can be a good sign. A caller who’s decided against booking might thank you and end the conversation. But someone who raises a concern may still be interested if you can address what’s bothering them.


You’ll hear some objections again and again. Here’s how to respond to four of them without putting pressure on your leads.


### “Let me talk to my spouse and call you back”


If a customer wants to talk it over with their spouse, send the estimate so they’re both looking at the same numbers. You can also pencil in a time, as long as they know it’s tentative until they confirm.


**Example response:** *“Totally fair. Want me to pencil you in for Thursday while you two talk it over? Can I check back tomorrow?”*


### “I’m getting a few other quotes”


Shopping around is a common tactic for customers to get the best deal, especially for a big job. Find out what else they’re weighing, like how soon you can start or what the warranty includes. Then text a written estimate so they can go through it line by line.


**Example response:** *“Sure. Besides price, what else are you comparing? I can text you our estimate so you can see what’s included.”*


### “That’s more than I expected”


A higher price can catch the caller off guard. If there are different ways to handle the job, lay out what each would cost. If waiting on a decision could make their existing problem worse, point that out to them.


**Example response:** *“I hear you. Depending on what we find, there may be a couple of ways to handle the repair. Want me to run through them with you?”*


### “Can I think about it and call you tomorrow?”


Before ending the conversation, ask what they still need to think about.


**Example response:** *“Of course. What part do you want to think through: the price, the timing, or something else?”*


Gracie has found that callers sometimes delay making a decision because their problem doesn’t feel urgent or they aren’t convinced the service is worth the price. If they raise a specific concern, address it while you have them on the phone.


### When to let it go


Good objection handling also means knowing when to stop. If you’ve asked what’s on their mind and they can’t name anything specific, ease off. Not every caller will move ahead with a booking, and pushing harder can sour things for next time. Ask whether you can check back later and agree on a time.


**Example response:** *“No problem. When would be a good time for me to check back?”*


##


7 Sales closing techniques to use on a sales call


The best way to close depends on the caller and the job, not on the script. These sales techniques are for[inbound sales](https://www.quo.com/blog/inbound-sales/) calls, when the customer calls you. Since they’ve already reached out, you can skip the hard push that comes with cold calling. Use this table to match what the caller says to the closing technique that fits.


What the caller says or does What it usually means Technique to try Example response


Describes an urgent problem, like water everywhere Needs help quickly Assumptive close “I can have someone there by 2. Does that work?”


Asks “What do you charge?” and shares no details Wants to understand the cost Good-better-best close “That depends on what’s going on. What’s the problem? Once I know, I can usually give you a ballpark number.”


Asks about scheduling, financing, or how long the job takes Close to a decision Assumptive close “I’ve got Thursday morning open. Want me to put you down?”


Mentions a spouse, landlord, or owner Needs someone else’s approval Summary close “So it’s the valve repair Thursday for $X. Would you like me to text that over so you can show them?”


Long call with lots of details Feeling a bit overwhelmed Summary close “So we can do the repair Thursday for $X. Would you like to book it?”


Gives short answers and is hard to read Unsure Question close “On a scale of 1 to 10, how ready are you to book? What would make it a 10?”


First-time caller who doesn’t know you yet Needs to trust you first Trial close “How about we start with a free estimate?”


Compares packages after hearing your estimate Weighing the options Good-better-best close “Would you like me to walk you through what’s included in each one?”


Asks weekly or biweekly, or morning or afternoon Interested and working out the details Alternative-choice close “Would mornings or afternoons work better for you?”


Has a real deadline, like a move-out or inspection On a tight timeline Urgency close “I have one opening before your inspection. Would you like it?”


### Assumptive close


When a caller asks, “When can you come out?” they may be close to booking. Instead of asking whether they want to book, start discussing appointment times.


**Examples:** *“What day works best for you?”* or *“Should I put you down for Tuesday morning?”*


**Best for:** Callers with an urgent problem or anyone asking about timing.


**Watch out:** Make sure the caller understands any visit fee before you book them.


### Summary close


For more complex and in-depth conversations, your leads may have a lot of information to remember.. In that case, the right approach is to recap the problem, the fix, the price, and the timing before asking if they want to book. Offer to text the summary so they have it handy.


**Examples:** *“So we’ll replace the water heater on Thursday for $X all in. Would you like to book that?”*


**Best for:** Longer calls and callers who need to check with someone else.


**Watch out:** Include every fee in the recap. A surprise charge later can damage the trust you’ve built.


### Trial close


First-time callers may hesitate to commit to a business they don’t know. A free estimate or consultation gives them a chance to learn about your service before committing to the full job. Use offers you already have, like crediting the visit fee toward the repair.


**Examples:** *“How about we start with a free estimate? If it works for you, we can schedule the job.”*


**Best for:** First-time callers, cleaning businesses, and law firms.


**Watch out:** Free estimates also attract price shoppers, so ask about the job before offering one. For law firms, consider making your first consultation free instead of discounting your actual services.


### Alternative-choice close


When a caller is ready to book, offer two choices that make scheduling easier for them. For cleaning businesses, that might mean weekly or every-other-week service. For a repair, it could be a morning or afternoon appointment.


**Examples:** *“Weekly or every other week?” or “Morning or afternoon?”*


**Best for:** Recurring services and scheduling.


**Watch out:** Only offer options you provide. Too many choices can make it harder for the caller to decide.


### Good-better-best close


If there’s more than one way to handle the job, lay out three options at three prices and let the caller pick. Highlight the tradeoffs for each approach so that customers are aware of what they’re signing up for.[ServiceTitan’s example](https://www.servicetitan.com/blog/good-better-best-hvac-proposal) shows how this works for a failed AC part. If the repair requires a full system replacement, the good-better-best approach outlines tradeoffs between cost, reliability, and energy efficiency. Structure these options so that it makes logical sense to choose the better option, and price it with enough margin for your business.


**Example:** *“We can replace the part for $X, replace it and clean the unit for $Y, or do both and add a maintenance plan for $Z. I’d recommend the middle one, since cleaning the unit helps the new part last longer. Which sounds right for you?”*


**Best for:** HVAC and plumbing repairs, replacements, and service packages.


**Watch out:** The basic option has to fix the problem on its own. If someone calls about a flooded basement, focus on getting help to them rather than discussing packages.


### Question close


On our calls, “Anything else for today?” came right at the end, leaving little time to address remaining concerns. Instead, ask what might stop them from booking while there’s time to talk it through.


**Example:** *“Anything on your mind before we book this?”*


**Best for:** Callers who seem interested but hesitant.


**Watch out:** Ask one question and let them answer. Too many questions turn the call into an interrogation.


### Urgency close


“Do you have a timeline in mind?” was the most-asked closing question on our team. It can help you see whether the caller needs the job done before a move-out, inspection, or holiday visit. If they do, offer an appointment that fits their deadline.


**Example:** *“You said the inspection is on the 15th. I have one opening before then. Would you like it?”*


You can also mention genuine scheduling limits, such as fewer openings when furnace calls pick up during the first cold snap.


**Best for:** Callers who need the job done before a specific date.


**Watch out:** Never invent a deadline. Fake scarcity backfires for businesses that live on reviews and word of mouth. Law firms should keep pressure out of intake and check their state bar’s advertising and solicitation rules.


##


Closing examples by industry


What does a good close sound like in your line of work? The steps are the same for every business, but what you’re putting on the calendar changes: a service visit, a consultation, or a first clean. Here’s how it plays out for home services, law firms, and cleaning businesses.


### Home services


Plumbers and HVAC companies get calls about no heating, water heater replacements, and failed AC units.


If it’s an emergency, qualify it immediately and route callers to your on-call team. A bigger project may need an on-site estimate before the customer can approve the work. Before confirming, get the caller’s address, contact number, and a quick description of the problem.


Here’s what you might say:


- *“I can have a tech there by 3 today. There’s a $X fee for the visit. Would you like me to book it?”*
- *“We’d need to see what’s going on before giving you a firm price. I have Thursday morning open for an estimate. Would that work?”*
- *“That comes to $X for parts and labor. If that works for you, I can put you on the schedule for Friday.”*


**Watch out:** Booking an estimate isn’t the same as booking the job. Make sure the caller knows which one they’re agreeing to and mention any visit fee up front.


### Law firms


People often call a law firm during a stressful time, so lead with empathy and avoid pressuring them. Most firms move from intake to a consultation, then to an engagement agreement if they take the case. Your goal on that first call is usually to book the consultation.


Before the caller gets into their story, collect the prospective client’s name and the names of other relevant parties. The firm needs these names to check for conflicts. Until that’s done, keep the case details brief. Under the American Bar Association’s[Rule 1.18](https://www.americanbar.org/groups/professional_responsibility/publications/model_rules_of_professional_conduct/rule_1_18_duties_of_prospective_client/) , certain information prospective clients share is protected even if the firm doesn’t take the case. Ask only what you need at this stage to avoid receiving sensitive information too early.


Here are three examples:


- *“I’m sorry you’re dealing with this. Before we get into details, can I get your full name and the names of any other people or businesses involved?”*
- *“Once we’ve checked for conflicts, we can book a consultation with one of our attorneys. Would Thursday or Friday work better?”*
- *“To clarify, booking a consultation doesn’t mean we’ve agreed to take your case. The attorney will talk through that with you.”*


**Watch out:** Never promise an outcome. Intake steps vary by state and firm, so check your state bar’s rules.


### Cleaning services


New callers usually open with “How much?” The answer depends on the home’s size, its condition, and how often they want service. The first clean often takes longer than regular visits, so it may be priced differently.


Ask whether they want a one-time clean or regular service, then book the first visit. For ongoing service, use the alternative-choice close. Let them choose between weekly and every-other-week visits.


You might say:


- *“Are you looking for a one-time clean, or regular service?”*
- *“The first clean is $X since it takes a bit longer. After that, would weekly or every other week work better?”*
- *“I can get your first clean on the calendar for Tuesday. Want me to set up every other week after that?”*


**Watch out:** Offer a recurring price only after you know the home’s size and condition. If the price could change once your team evaluates the space, say so on the call.


##


Common sales call closing mistakes


A call can feel like it went well and still end without a booking. Here are nine mistakes owners and sales reps make, along with ways to avoid them:


1. **Letting calls go to voicemail during jobs.** This mistake impacts your ability to take incoming calls. When you’re on a job, you might not be available to talk to new leads. Instead of risking losing these leads to the competition, use a shared number to route calls to available team members. Or route them to a 24×7 answering service like Sona.
2. **Only closing at the end.** If you wait until the last minute to ask for the job, the caller may already be mentally done with the call. Check in along the way with micro-close questions like: *“Does that sound right to you?”*
3. **Ending on “Anything else for today?”** It sounds polite, but it often gets a quick “Nope, that’s it” and a goodbye. Swap it for a more definitive closing question like: *“What else should we cover before I get you on the schedule?”*
4. **Sending an estimate and not following up.** It’s easy to send an estimate and never hear from leads again. Before you send an estimate, agree to a follow-up schedule on your calls. Add the date to your CRM or calendar so you stick to it.
5. **Leaving the next step in their court.** Ending with “let me know” or “call us when you’re ready” sounds friendly, but it leaves the next step up to the caller. Instead, offer a tentative time before the call ends.
6. **Ignoring the awkward feeling.** Asking to book can feel awkward, even when the caller seems ready. Rather than skipping the question, ask whether the caller has any concerns: *“Is there anything about the price or the work you’re unsure about?”*
7. **Discounting before you know they’re ready.** A pause after you share pricing doesn’t always mean it’s too expensive. Cut your price too soon, and you give away margin you didn’t need to. Find out where they stand first: *“If I can get you in this week, would you like to go ahead?”*
8. **Talking past the close.** When a caller agrees to book, the sale is over. If you keep talking about your warranty or how long you’ve been in business, you give them new reasons to think twice.
9. **Pushing too hard.** Leaning on a hesitant caller often gets you the opposite of a booking. Earn the ask first by explaining the fix and talking through their concerns. If they still need time, agree on when you’ll follow up.


##


What to do after you hang up


Even if you close a call effectively, it doesn’t matter until you provide the service and invoice your customers. That’s when you need to follow through. Send a quick recap text or email the same day. If they called about a leaky kitchen sink, remind them what you discussed and the price you quoted. That way, they have something to look at when they’re ready to decide.


Keep your own record of the call, too. Add the job details and next steps to your job management software or contact notes. Label your calls with[call tags](https://www.quo.com/product/ai/call-tagging) like“Estimate sent,” “Booked,” “Needs follow-up,” or “Price shopper” so you can see at a glance where each caller stands.


Remembering every detail isn’t easy when you’re taking calls between jobs. Quo’s[AI call summaries](https://www.quo.com/features/call-summary) can help you keep track without stopping to take notes while you’re working.


The calls that didn’t book are worth a second listen. Go through a few[call recordings](https://www.quo.com/product/call-recording) each week. Did you miss a question, or did the customer raise a concern you didn’t address? Reviewing them is useful sales training for you and anyone else who answers your phone. Share the best examples with your team as part of regular[call coaching](https://www.quo.com/blog/call-coaching/) so everyone learns from the same calls. You can also save time on call coaching with[Quo Agent](https://www.quo.com/product/quo-agent) , our AI assistant. Ask specific questions about your calls, and Quo Agent can highlight what went well and where your reps can do better.


*Spot call coaching opportunities in Quo using Quo Agent.*


### A simple follow-up schedule for estimates


Plenty of people take a few days to decide after getting an estimate. A simple follow-up schedule helps you stay in touch without bugging them:


- **Same day.** Send the estimate with your recap. Mention when you’ll call next, so they know to expect you. *“Hi Dana, here’s the estimate for the water heater repair we talked about. I’ll give you a ring Thursday in case anything comes up.”*
- **Day 2.** Make the call. If they don’t answer, follow up with a short text. *“Hi Dana, did anything in the estimate raise questions? I’m glad to walk you through it.”*
- **Day 7.** Try one more time. *“Wanted to see if you’d still like to get this done. Happy to hold a spot.”*
- **After that.** Let it rest. Put them on your seasonal or maintenance reminder list.


In traditional B2B sales, where the sales funnel is often longer, you’ll hear about the 2-2-2 rule: follow up after 2 days, 2 weeks, and 2 months. Local service jobs have a shorter sales cycle, so follow up sooner while customers are still deciding.


##


Close more sales calls with Quo


Remember the homeowner with the leaking water heater? If you’d asked who else needed to weigh in and agreed on a time to follow up, you might have had a booking instead of waiting for a callback that never came.


Closing calls well means building toward the booking throughout the conversation. But you need to catch the call in the first place. Quo can help with both:


- **Missed calls.** When you’re busy on a job, Sona can answer for you. Missed-call text-backs give potential clients another way to reach you before they try the next business.
- **Team coverage.** With a[shared number](https://www.quo.com/product/shared-numbers) , your team sees the same calls and texts. Whoever’s free can take over without making the customer repeat everything.

FAQs


**What’s the best way to close a sales call?**


Work toward the booking from the start instead of saving one big ask for the end. Find out what’s wrong, when they need it fixed, and who else gets a say.


Once you understand the problem, explain the fix and what it’ll cost. Address concerns before offering a time. By the end, you should have a booking or an agreed-upon next step.


**What do you say at the end of a sales call?**


It depends on whether the customer has booked. If they have, confirm the day, arrival window, and address. Then text them the details so they have everything in writing. If they’re still deciding, ask, *“What else should we cover before I get you on the schedule?”* Agree on when you’ll follow up before the call ends.


**How do you close a sale without being pushy?**


Explain the fix in plain words and talk through concerns before asking for the booking. Give customers options when appropriate, like a basic repair or a full replacement, so they can choose what fits their needs and budget.


You don’t need pressure to seal the deal. If they need time, agree on a day to follow up rather than pushing for an answer.


**What is a sales closing strategy?**


A sales closing strategy is your plan for the commitment you’re asking for on a call and when you’ll ask for it.


For a new caller with a leak, that might be a booked visit. For someone you sent an estimate to last week, it might be a yes or a no on the quote. Knowing the goal helps you ask the right questions throughout the conversation.


**What are some examples of sales closing questions?**


Good closing questions help you determine whether the customer is ready to book. Here are four you can use on service calls:
• *“Do you have a timeline in mind?”*
• *“Do you need to run this by anyone else first?”*
• *“Is there anything that would stop you from booking today?”*
• *“Would you like me to get you on the schedule?”*


**How many times should you follow up before giving up on a lead?**


For a typical home service estimate, two follow-ups over the next week are a reasonable starting point. Send the quote and a recap the same day, give them a call around day two to see what they think, then check in once more around day seven.


If they still don’t respond, leave it there. You can reach out later with a relevant seasonal or maintenance reminder.
